pitch_01: For months we have pitched one3seven as intake software for law firms. That undersells it, badly. We built something the market does not have a clean name for yet. In the next few minutes I will show you the arithmetic, the full picture against every other AI intake tool, and exactly why a hesitant firm should say yes.
pitch_02: Start with the enemy. Every employment case begins the same broken way. A wronged worker walks in with pay stubs in a drawer and screenshots on a phone. Then an attorney burns ninety minutes doing a cold read of a stranger's mess, and decides in the dark whether there is a case worth taking. That ninety minutes is unbillable. You cannot bill a prospect you have not signed. It is pure cost.
pitch_03: And we are not guessing this works. Victoria ran this exact method on her own insurance claim. She organized the record herself, handed it to the lawyers, and settled at the maximum. In a pre-revenue company, that lived proof is worth more than a traction slide.
pitch_04: Here is the discipline that makes this sell. Firms do not buy new categories. They buy a better version of a thing they already understand. So to a firm we say, plainly, the fastest and most compliant way to screen a case. The bigger story, the worker-owned system of record, is how we talk to investors. Same product, two frames.
pitch_05: Now the math. On conservative, firm-editable assumptions, screening one intake the traditional way takes about ninety minutes. With a generic A-I intake tool that summarizes but does not link to sources, you still have to verify everything, so call it fifty-five minutes. With one3seven, the attorney opens a source-linked record, a decision card, and a coverage rate, and reaches a screening decision in about eighteen minutes.
pitch_06: Turn that into throughput. Say a firm gives ten hours a week to screening new intakes. The traditional way, that is about seven intakes a week. With a top A-I intake tool, about eleven. With one3seven, about thirty-three. That is roughly five times the traditional pace, and three times the best A-I tool, from the same ten hours.
pitch_07: Here is the part a hesitant firm needs to hear. That screening time is unbillable, so every minute we save is margin you get back. At a blended ninety dollars an hour and twenty-five intakes a month, one3seven saves about thirty hours, or twenty-seven hundred dollars, every month. The Firm tier costs five hundred forty-nine. On stingy assumptions it is a wash. On realistic ones it returns four to five times its price, before a single extra case is signed.
pitch_08: What earns that eighteen minutes is the Claim Lens. Pick a legal theory, and the record re-sorts around that claim's statutory elements. For each element we show every matching item with its source, and we show, loudly, what is missing. It is a coverage map, not a verdict. It never says you have a case. It shows you what is on file and what is not.
pitch_09: And every fact is one click from the page it came from. You are going to fact-check the record anyway. We just make it instant. No hunting through a P-D-F. That is why we are safe and trustworthy. one3seven organizes and cites. It never concludes. The attorney decides. That is exactly the pattern California's A-B three sixteen rewards, the burden stays on the lawyer, and everything we surface is auditable back to a source.
pitch_10: So here is the full picture against a known A-I intake tool. They give you a summary you cannot trust without re-reading everything. We give you source-linked facts, a coverage rate no competitor computes, and an output that is provably non-concluding. They automate a form. We deliver a review-ready file.
pitch_11: But the deepest difference is not the intake. It is the ecosystem around the worker. A generic tool is a form the worker fills once and abandons. one3seven is a journey the worker owns and maintains, free, with reminders, records requests, and their own mitigation log. A worker who owns their record is far more willing to cooperate, and a cooperative worker gives you a more complete file with fewer follow-up cycles. Better inputs, automatically, over eighteen to thirty-six months.
pitch_12: And the work compounds. The same organized, source-linked record that screens the case in eighteen minutes is the spine of the demand letter and the mediation brief. We are not promising a faster verdict. We are removing the rework between every stage, so the hours you invest once keep paying off downstream.
pitch_13: Why now, and not next year. Legal A-I did two point one billion dollars in the first half of twenty twenty-six. Attorney fear of A-I is peaking, which gives us a narrow window to be the trusted teacher instead of the threat. And nobody has planted a flag in the compliant, California, worker-first niche. The window is open now.
pitch_14: So here is what each of you owns. Revenue, the money rails and the accounts-payable packet that unblocks the first check. Sales, our beachhead of small California plaintiff firms, won through a founder-led fifteen-minute intake review, anchored on value, not software cost. Operations, instrument the funnel, keep the data clean, and hold the privacy wall that keeps worker files out of analytics. One number aligns all three, intakes routed and actioned per firm, per week.
pitch_15: Let me close honestly, because you will poke holes and you should. Three gates stand before a paying firm. One server-side fix, counsel sign-off, and the founders' agreement with clean I-P. We go big on the story today, and we hold those three gates. In one line. We did not build better intake software. We built the record the entire system was missing. Now let's go take the position we already earned.
